Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire, never opened any book for his own pleasure except the Baronetage. It supplied employment in an idle hour and comfort in an unhappy one. Its scant surviving examples of the oldest patents awakened his powers of admiration and reverence; its almost interminable new creations of the previous century transformed unpleasant feelings about domestic matters into contempt and pity. And should all the other pages fail him, he could turn to his own history with unfailing interest. His favourite volume invariably fell open at this entry:

“Elliot of Kellynch Hall.

“Walter Elliot, born on March 1, 1760; married on July 15, 1784, to Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq., of South Park, Gloucestershire. By this lady, who died in 1800, he has issue: Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a son still-born on November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

Thus, precisely, the paragraph had first emerged from the printer; but Sir Walter had embellished it, for his family’s information and his own, by appending after Mary’s birth: “Married on December 16, 1810, to Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq., of Uppercross, Somersetshire.” He had also entered, with scrupulous accuracy, the day of the month upon which his wife had died.

Next came the customary account of this old and respectable family’s history and advancement: its original settlement in Cheshire; its appearance in Dugdale; service as high sheriff; representation of a borough through three successive parliaments; demonstrations of loyalty; and elevation to the baronetcy in the first year of Charles II. Together with every Mary and Elizabeth they had married, it occupied two handsome duodecimo pages, ending with the arms and motto, and “Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, Somersetshire.” Sir Walter’s pen again supplied the final addition:

“Heir presumptive: William Walter Elliot, Esq., great-grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity began and ended Sir Walter Elliot’s character: pride in his looks and pride in his position. As a young man he had been exceptionally handsome; at fifty-four he remained a very fine figure. Few women bestowed greater thought upon their appearance, and no newly created lord’s valet could have taken more delight in his social standing. He ranked the gift of beauty immediately below the gift of a baronetcy; and Sir Walter Elliot, who possessed both, continually commanded his own most devoted admiration.

His handsome face and his rank had, at least, one legitimate claim upon his affection: they must have secured him a wife whose character was far superior to anything his own deserved.

I wish to see you settled among desirable connections, and for that purpose it is best to retain as few unsuitable acquaintances as possible. Therefore I say that, should you still be in this neighbourhood when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your friendship with his sisters will not lead you into knowing his wife. She will most likely be nothing but some farmer’s daughter, quite uneducated.”

“Certainly. Yes. Though I cannot imagine Mr. Martin marrying anybody who had not received some education—and been brought up very properly. Still, I would not put my judgment against yours, and I am sure I shall have no wish to know his wife. I shall always feel a great affection for the Miss Martins, particularly Elizabeth, and should be very sorry to abandon them, since they are every bit as well educated as I am. But if he marries an exceedingly ignorant and vulgar woman, then of course I had better avoid visiting her, if possible.”

Emma observed her throughout the changes of this speech and detected no disturbing sign of love. The young man had been her earliest admirer, but Emma hoped he possessed no further claim, and that Harriet would present no serious obstacle to any friendly scheme she herself might form.

On the very next day, walking along the Donwell road, they encountered Mr. Martin. He was afoot, and after regarding Emma with great respect, turned upon her companion a look of perfectly sincere pleasure. Emma welcomed this opportunity to inspect him. She strolled a few yards ahead while they conversed, and her quick observation soon gave her a sufficient knowledge of Mr. Robert Martin. He was exceedingly neat and had the air of a sensible young fellow, but his appearance offered no additional attractions. She thought that once Harriet compared him with gentlemen, he must forfeit whatever place he had won in her affections. Harriet was not blind to manners: of her own accord she had remarked upon Emma’s father’s gentleness, with admiration mingled with surprise. Mr. Martin looked as though he had never heard of manners.

Their conversation lasted only a few minutes, since Miss Woodhouse must not be left waiting. Harriet then hurried to join her, smiling and in a flutter of excitement which Miss Woodhouse hoped shortly to quiet.

“Just think of our meeting him like that! How very strange! He said it was the merest accident that he had not taken the way round by Randalls. He had no idea we ever walked along this road. He supposed we went towards Randalls nearly every day.”

Mr. Darcy praised his sister’s musical skill with affection.

“I am very pleased to hear she is doing so well,” said Lady Catherine. “And please tell her from me that she cannot expect to become excellent unless she practises a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he replied, “that she needs no such advice. She practises very regularly.”

“So much the better. One cannot practise too much. When I next write to her, I shall tell her she must never neglect it. I often tell young ladies that no one can become an excellent musician without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play really well unless she practises more. And although Mrs. Collins has no instrument, Miss Bennet is very welcome, as I have often said, to come to Rosings every day and use the piano in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. She would not be in anyone’s way in that part of the house, you know.”

Mr. Darcy looked slightly embarrassed by his aunt’s bad manners and did not reply.

After coffee, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth that she had promised to play for him. She went straight to the piano, and he pulled a chair close to her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song before returning to her conversation with her other nephew. Eventually he walked away from her and approached the piano with his usual unhurried manner. He stood where he could see the young woman’s face clearly. Elizabeth noticed his movement. At the first suitable pause, she turned towards him with a teasing smile and said,

“You intend to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming so grandly to listen. But I refuse to be frightened, even though your sister plays so well. I am too stubborn to let other people scare me whenever they choose. Every attempt to intimidate me only makes me braver.”

“I will not say that you are mistaken,” he answered, “because you cannot really believe I mean to frighten you. Besides, I have had the pleasure of knowing you long enough to understand that you sometimes enjoy claiming to hold opinions that are not actually yours.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this description of herself. Then she said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, “Your cousin will give you a very fine impression of me and teach you not to believe a word I say. How particularly unlucky I am to meet someone who can expose my true character so well, in a place where I had hoped to give a reasonably good account of myself.”
